body_html:
Spanish confusing words are the pairs that make learners hesitate in the middle of a sentence: pedir or preguntar? Llevar or traer? Pero or sino? Most of them exist because English uses one word where Spanish uses two. After ten years translating between English and Spanish, I see the same pairs cause the same mistakes again and again, so I have collected all of them here. Each one comes with a one-line rule, real examples, a memory tip and a link to a full guide with conversations and an interactive quiz.

Key takeaways
  • Most confusing pairs exist because one English word splits into two Spanish words.
  • Each pair can be solved with one question, such as “is it coming here or going there?”
  • Accent marks create a separate group of look-alikes: si and sí, tu and tú.
  • Learn each pair through whole sentences, not translations of single words.
{{toc}}

Why Spanish confusing words happen

There are three reasons a pair of Spanish words feels confusing, and knowing which one you are dealing with makes it much easier to fix.

  • English has one word, Spanish has two. “Ask”, “know”, “play”, “leave” and “but” each split into two or more Spanish words. This is the biggest group.
  • The words look or sound alike. Haber and a ver sound identical; hecho and echo differ only by a silent letter.
  • An accent mark changes the word. Si and sí, esta and está: the same letters, but different meanings.

The first group is about meaning, so you need to understand the idea behind each word. The second and third are about spelling, so a simple test usually solves them.

Spanish confusing words at a glance

Here is every pair in this series with the one question that decides it. Bookmark this table and come back to it when you hesitate.

Verb pairs

Verb pairs are the largest and most important group, because verbs carry the meaning of the sentence. Choosing the wrong one rarely makes you impossible to understand, but it does make you sound translated.

Pedir vs preguntar

Both mean “to ask”. Pedir is asking for something: an object, a favor, food. Preguntar is asking a question to get information.

  • Le pedí un favor a mi vecino. (I asked my neighbor for a favor.)
  • Le pregunté a qué hora abre la tienda. (I asked him what time the store opens.)

Memory tip: if you could replace “ask” with “request”, use pedir. Full guide: {{link:pedir-vs-preguntar|pedir vs preguntar}}.

Llevar vs traer

Traer is movement toward the speaker, like “bring”. Llevar is movement away from the speaker, like “take”. The tricky part is that English often says “bring” where Spanish needs llevar.

  • ¿Puedes traer pan cuando vengas? (Can you bring bread when you come?)
  • Voy a llevar vino a la fiesta de Ana. (I’ll bring wine to Ana’s party.)

Memory tip: ask “is it coming here, or going there?” Full guide: {{link:llevar-vs-traer|llevar vs traer}}.

Ir vs venir

This pair follows the same logic. Venir means coming to where the speaker is; ir means going anywhere else. When someone calls you to dinner, you answer ¡Ya voy!, not “ya vengo”, because you are going to where they are.

  • ¿Vienes a mi casa esta noche? (Are you coming to my place tonight?)
  • Mañana voy a tu casa. (I’m coming to your place tomorrow.)

Memory tip: Spanish always looks at the trip from the speaker’s position. Full guide: {{link:ir-vs-venir|ir vs venir}}.

Mirar vs ver

Mirar is to look at something on purpose. Ver is to see, and it is also the everyday verb for watching TV or a movie.

  • ¡Mira ese pájaro! (Look at that bird!)
  • Anoche vimos una película. (We watched a movie last night.)

Memory tip: eyes pointed with intention is mirar; everything else is usually ver. Full guide: {{link:mirar-vs-ver|mirar vs ver}}.

Oír vs escuchar

Oír is to hear, without trying. Escuchar is to listen, with attention. On a bad phone line you say ¿Me oyes?; with music you escuchas.

  • Oí un ruido en la cocina. (I heard a noise in the kitchen.)
  • Escucho un podcast en el carro. (I listen to a podcast in the car.)

Memory tip: escuchar already includes “to”, so never say “escuchar a la música”. Full guide: {{link:oir-vs-escuchar|oír vs escuchar}}.

Tocar vs jugar

Jugar is to play a game or sport. Tocar is to play an instrument, and also to touch, and even “to be someone’s turn”.

  • Juego al fútbol los sábados. (I play soccer on Saturdays.)
  • Mi hija toca el piano. (My daughter plays the piano.)

Memory tip: if it makes music, it is tocar. Full guide: {{link:tocar-vs-jugar|tocar vs jugar}}.

Quedar vs quedarse

Quedarse means to stay or to keep something. Quedar has several jobs: to be located, to fit, to be left, and, especially in Spain, to arrange to meet.

  • Me quedo en casa hoy. (I’m staying home today.)
  • Esta camisa me queda grande. (This shirt is too big on me.)

Memory tip: the pronoun often signals “stay”; without it, think “fit, be left, be located”. Full guide: {{link:quedar-vs-quedarse|quedar vs quedarse}}.

Salir vs irse vs dejar

All three can translate “leave”. Salir is to go out of a place, irse is to leave or go away, and dejar is to leave something or someone behind.

  • Salgo de la oficina a las seis. (I leave the office at six.)
  • Me voy, ¡nos vemos mañana! (I’m off, see you tomorrow!)
  • Dejé las llaves en el carro. (I left the keys in the car.)

Memory tip: if there is an object you left behind, it is always dejar. Full guide: {{link:salir-vs-irse|salir vs irse vs dejar}}.

Ponerse, volverse, hacerse

English uses “become” or “get” for every change. Spanish chooses by type of change. Ponerse is quick and temporary, often emotions or color. Volverse is a deep, usually involuntary change of character. Hacerse is a change you work for, like a profession.

  • Se puso nerviosa antes del examen. (She got nervous before the exam.)
  • Se volvió muy serio después del accidente. (He became very serious after the accident.)
  • Se hizo médico a los 30. (He became a doctor at 30.)

Memory tip: quick mood, ponerse; deep change, volverse; effort, hacerse. Full guide: {{link:ponerse-volverse-hacerse|ponerse, volverse, hacerse}}.

Saber vs conocer

Both mean “to know”. Saber is for facts, information and skills. Conocer is for people, places and things you are familiar with through experience.

  • Sé dónde vive. (I know where she lives.)
  • Conozco a su hermana. (I know her sister.)

Memory tip: if you could add “about” or “how to”, it is saber; if you have met it, it is conocer. Full guide: {{link:saber-vs-conocer|saber vs conocer}}.

Tener vs haber

Tener is to have, as in possession. Haber is mostly an auxiliary verb (he comido, I have eaten) and, in the form hay, means “there is” or “there are”.

  • Tengo dos hermanos. (I have two brothers.)
  • Hay mucha gente en el parque. (There are a lot of people in the park.)

Memory tip: “there is” and “there are” are always hay, singular or plural. Full guide: {{link:tener-vs-haber|tener vs haber}}.

Poder vs saber

“Can” has two Spanish versions. Poder is about being able to right now, or having permission. Saber plus an infinitive is about a skill you have learned.

  • Sé nadar. (I can swim, I know how.)
  • Hoy no puedo nadar, me duele el hombro. (I can’t swim today, my shoulder hurts.)

Memory tip: learned skill, saber; circumstances, poder. Full guide: {{link:poder-vs-saber|poder vs saber}}.

Decir vs hablar

Decir is to say or tell, and it focuses on the content. Hablar is to speak or talk, and it focuses on the activity.

  • Me dijo que estaba cansado. (He told me he was tired.)
  • Hablo con mi mamá todos los domingos. (I talk to my mom every Sunday.)

Memory tip: if you can quote the words, use decir. Full guide: {{link:decir-vs-hablar|decir vs hablar}}.

Volver vs devolver

Volver is to come back or go back. Devolver is to give something back or return an item to a store. Volver a plus an infinitive also means “to do again”.

  • Vuelvo a las cinco. (I’ll be back at five.)
  • Tengo que devolver estos zapatos. (I have to return these shoes.)

Memory tip: people vuelven; things are devueltas. Full guide: {{link:volver-vs-devolver|volver vs devolver}}.

Grammar pairs

These pairs are about structure rather than vocabulary: which word connects two ideas, which pronoun to use and how to ask a question. Three of the biggest grammar questions each have their own guide: {{link:por-vs-para|por vs para}}, {{link:preterite-vs-imperfect|preterite vs imperfect}} and {{link:indicative-vs-subjunctive|indicative vs subjunctive}}.

Pero vs sino

Pero adds a contrast: both ideas are true. Sino corrects a negative statement: not this, but that. Before a conjugated verb, use sino que.

  • Es caro, pero es muy bueno. (It’s expensive, but it’s very good.)
  • No es mexicano, sino colombiano. (He isn’t Mexican, he’s Colombian.)

Memory tip: if the first part has no and the second replaces it, use sino. Full guide: {{link:pero-vs-sino|pero vs sino}}.

Tú vs usted

Both mean “you”. Tú is informal, for friends, family, children and people your age in relaxed settings. Usted is formal, for strangers, older people and professional situations. In Latin America, ustedes is the plural for everyone.

  • ¿Cómo estás? (to a friend)
  • ¿Cómo está usted? (to your partner’s grandmother)

Memory tip: when in doubt, start with usted and let the other person invite you to use tú. Full guide: {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

Qué vs cuál

Both can mean “what”. With ser, ¿Qué es…? asks for a definition, while ¿Cuál es…? asks you to pick or give a specific item. That is why you ask ¿Cuál es tu número?, not “qué es tu número”.

  • ¿Qué es un aguacate? (What is an avocado?)
  • ¿Cuál es tu dirección? (What is your address?)

Memory tip: definition, qué; selection, cuál. Full guide: {{link:que-vs-cual|qué vs cuál}}.

Porque, por qué, porqué, por que

¿Por qué? is “why?”, porque is “because”, el porqué is a noun meaning “the reason”, and por que is a rare combination meaning “for which”.

  • ¿Por qué llegas tarde? (Why are you late?)
  • Porque había tráfico. (Because there was traffic.)

Memory tip: questions split it in two with an accent; answers keep it together. Full guide: {{link:porque-vs-por-que|porque vs por qué}}.

Este, ese, aquel

Spanish has three distances where English has two. Este is near me, ese is near you, and aquel is far from both of us.

  • Este café está frío. (This coffee, here with me, is cold.)
  • ¿Me pasas ese libro? (Can you pass me that book, by you?)
  • Aquella casa es de mi tía. (That house, over there, is my aunt’s.)

Memory tip: here, there, over there. Full guide: {{link:este-ese-aquel|este, ese, aquel}}.

Aquí vs acá

Both mean “here”. Aquí is slightly more precise and common everywhere; acá is a little more vague and very common in Latin America, especially with movement.

  • Vivo aquí desde 2019. (I’ve lived here since 2019.)
  • ¡Ven acá! (Come here!)

Memory tip: you can’t go wrong with aquí, but acá sounds natural in Mexico. Full guide: {{link:aqui-vs-aca|aquí vs acá}}.

Lo vs le

Lo (and la) replaces a direct object: the thing or person that receives the action. Le replaces an indirect object: the person who receives something. In parts of Spain, le is also used for male people as direct objects.

  • ¿El libro? Lo compré ayer. (The book? I bought it yesterday.)
  • Le di el libro a Juan. (I gave Juan the book.)

Memory tip: if you can add “to” or “for” in English, it’s usually le. Full guide: {{link:lo-vs-le|lo vs le}}.

Adjectives and adverbs

English often lets one word do two jobs (“I’m good”, “that was good”). Spanish is stricter: adjectives describe nouns and change their endings, while adverbs describe verbs and never change.

Bueno vs bien

Bueno is an adjective that describes a noun. Bien is an adverb that describes how something is done or how someone feels. Before a masculine singular noun, bueno shortens to buen.

  • Es un buen restaurante. (It’s a good restaurant.)
  • Cocinas muy bien. (You cook very well.)

Memory tip: careful with está bueno about a person: it means attractive. Full guide: {{link:bueno-vs-bien|bueno vs bien}}.

Muy vs mucho

Muy goes before adjectives and adverbs. Mucho goes with nouns (and agrees with them) or after verbs. Never combine them as “muy mucho”.

  • Estoy muy cansado. (I’m very tired.)
  • Trabajo mucho y tengo muchas reuniones. (I work a lot and I have a lot of meetings.)

Memory tip: “very” is muy; “a lot” and “many” are mucho. Full guide: {{link:muy-vs-mucho|muy vs mucho}}.

Malo vs mal

This mirrors bueno and bien. Malo describes a noun, mal describes an action or a state, and malo shortens to mal before a masculine singular noun.

  • Tuve un mal día. (I had a bad day.)
  • Me siento mal. (I feel bad.)

Memory tip: if “bien” would fit, use “mal”. Full guide: {{link:malo-vs-mal|malo vs mal}}.

También vs tampoco

También agrees with a positive statement: “me too”. Tampoco agrees with a negative one: “me neither”.

  • —Me gusta el café. —A mí también.
  • —No me gusta el té. —A mí tampoco.

Memory tip: match the mood of the first sentence. Full guide: {{link:tambien-vs-tampoco|también vs tampoco}}.

Ya vs todavía

Ya means already or now. Todavía means still, and with a negative, yet. Ya no means “no longer”, and todavía no means “not yet”.

  • Ya comí. (I’ve already eaten.)
  • Todavía no he terminado. (I haven’t finished yet.)

Memory tip: ya no is a change; todavía no is a wait. Full guide: {{link:ya-vs-todavia|ya vs todavía}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Look-alike words: accents that change meaning

This group is about writing. In speech, the context almost always makes the meaning clear, but in a message or an email a missing accent can change what you say. The Real Academia Española explains the rule for these accents, called the tilde diacrítica, in its Diccionario panhispánico de dudas. There are also guides to {{link:el-vs-el|el vs él}}, {{link:mas-vs-mas|mas vs más}} and {{link:solo-vs-solo|solo vs sólo}}. For the bigger picture, see {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}.

Si vs sí

Si without an accent means “if”. Sí with an accent means “yes”, and it can also be a pronoun meaning “himself” or “herself”.

  • Si llueve, me quedo en casa. (If it rains, I’ll stay home.)
  • Sí, claro. (Yes, of course.)

Memory tip: yes is strong, so it gets the accent. Full guide: {{link:si-vs-si|si vs sí}}.

Tu vs tú

Tu is the possessive “your”. Tú is the pronoun “you”.

  • ¿Es tu carro? (Is it your car?)
  • Tú tienes razón. (You’re right.)

Memory tip: a noun after it means no accent. Full guide: {{link:tu-vs-tu|tu vs tú}}.

Esta vs está

Esta means “this” before a feminine noun. Está is a form of estar, meaning “is”.

  • Esta casa es nueva. (This house is new.)
  • La casa está lejos. (The house is far.)

Memory tip: if you can replace it with “is”, it needs the accent. Full guide: {{link:esta-vs-esta|esta vs está}}.

Hecho vs echo

The silent h separates two verbs. Hecho comes from hacer (done, made, a fact). Echo comes from echar (I throw, pour or put in).

  • He hecho la tarea. (I’ve done the homework.)
  • Le echo sal a la sopa. (I put salt in the soup.)

Memory tip: after he, has, ha, it is always hecho. Full guide: {{link:hecho-vs-echo|hecho vs echo}}.

Haber vs a ver

They sound identical. Haber is a verb (there to be, to have). A ver means “let’s see”.

  • A ver, ¿qué pasó? (Let’s see, what happened?)
  • Tiene que haber un error. (There must be a mistake.)

Memory tip: if you could say “let’s see”, write it as two words. Full guide: {{link:haber-vs-a-ver|haber vs a ver}}.

The pairs I correct most as a translator

When I review Spanish written by learners, a few pairs come up far more often than the rest.

  • Pedir vs preguntar in emails. “I would like to ask for a meeting” becomes quisiera preguntar por una reunión, which sounds like you want information about a meeting. You want quisiera pedir una reunión.
  • Llevar vs traer when making plans. “I’ll bring the kids to your house” is llevaré a los niños a tu casa if you are the one speaking from your own home.
  • Saber vs conocer with cities. ¿Sabes Chicago? is a common slip. You want ¿Conoces Chicago?
  • Pero vs sino in corrections. Learners almost never use sino, so their corrections sound unfinished: No quiero té, sino café.

If you only study four pairs this month, make it these four. They also appear among the {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|common Spanish mistakes}} learners make in every area, not just vocabulary.

How to learn Spanish confusing words

1. Learn one pair at a time

Read one guide, take its quiz, and use the pair in your own sentences for a few days before moving to the next. Studying ten pairs in one evening only mixes them up further.

2. Learn the idea, not the translation

“Llevar means take” will fail you the first time English says “bring”. “Llevar is movement away from me” will not. Every guide in this series starts with the idea behind each word for this reason.

3. Collect real sentences

When you meet one of these words in a book, a song or a show, write down the whole sentence. A notebook of real examples beats any rule. I explain the method in {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}.

4. Say your sentences out loud

These pairs are mostly a speaking problem, because there is no time to think in conversation. Saying a few model sentences aloud each day builds the automatic choice you need. Reading in parallel English and Spanish helps too, because you see exactly where the two languages split; see {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}}.

Final thoughts

Spanish confusing words are not a sign that Spanish is illogical. They are a sign that Spanish notices differences English ignores: whether you are asking for something or about something, whether you know a fact or a person, whether something is coming or going. Once you see the idea behind each pair, the choice becomes natural. Start with the table above, pick one pair, and take its quiz today.

faq.q: What are the most confusing words in Spanish?
faq.a: The pairs learners mix up most are pedir and preguntar, saber and conocer, llevar and traer, ser and estar, por and para, and pero and sino.

faq.q: Why are some Spanish words so confusing?
faq.a: Usually because English uses one word where Spanish uses two, each with a narrower meaning. Others look or sound alike, or differ only by an accent mark.

faq.q: Is it a big problem if I mix them up?
faq.a: Usually not. People will understand you from context. But mixing them up makes your Spanish sound translated, and a few, such as está bueno about a person, can change your meaning.

faq.q: Do Spanish speakers confuse these words too?
faq.a: The spelling pairs, yes: haber and a ver, hecho and echo, or porque and por qué are common slips in native writing. The meaning pairs are typical of learners.

faq.q: What is the best way to learn Spanish confusing words?
faq.a: Learn the idea behind each word rather than a translation, study one pair at a time, collect real example sentences and test yourself with a quiz.

faq.q: Which pair should I learn first?
faq.a: Start with saber vs conocer and pedir vs preguntar. They appear constantly in conversation, and the rule for each is simple.

questions.q: ¿Me puedes ___ un vaso de agua?
questions.explain: The water is coming toward the speaker: traer.

questions.q: Le voy a ___ a qué hora llega.
questions.explain: You want information, so it is preguntar.
People are known through experience: conocer.

questions.q: No es mi novio, ___ mi primo.
questions.explain: A correction after a negative: sino.
